Flood Insurance Data

The NFIP in numbers

The National Flood Insurance Program had 4,529,364 policy units in force on August 31, 2026. Existing single-family primary-home policies cost a median of $1,066 a year, premium plus fees. Since 1978 FEMA's records list 2,680,429 NFIP claims, paid or not, and $88,422,296,888 paid in total on them.

How does the NFIP work?

Federal flood insurance (NFIP) is sold only in communities that take part in the NFIP; in a community that has not joined, or once a suspension takes effect, no one can buy an NFIP policy. For a home, NFIP building coverage goes up to $250,000 and contents coverage up to $100,000; a renter's contents coverage goes up to $100,000; for a business, building and contents each go up to $500,000. Most NFIP policies take effect 30 days after you buy, so a policy bought today will not cover a flood this week.

To buy: call the NFIP at (877) 336-2627, go to FloodSmart.gov, or ask any licensed insurance agent. Every NFIP insurer offers the same rates.

Congress has to keep renewing the NFIP's authority. During a lapse, NFIP policies cannot be bought, renewed or increased until the authority returns. Policies already in force run to their expiration date and claims on them are still handled, though FEMA says the money to pay claims may be limited.

A private flood policy can meet a lender's flood requirement: federally regulated lenders must accept a private policy that meets the federal definition of private flood insurance and covers at least what the loan requires (12 CFR §339.3(c)). Its price is not in FEMA's records.

What these numbers cannot tell you

Your premium, private insurers' prices, or why a price changed. The median is what existing policies pay, not a quote.
